questions.q: Which reason for a king to expand his kingdom into an empire is listed in the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter lists ambition to rule the whole world, access to resources for economic and military strength, and a desire for great wealth. Empires had diverse people and still needed an army and administration.
o: To gain access to resources for economic and military strength
To make every language and custom of his subjects identical
To avoid paying tribute to a stronger neighbouring ruler
To end the need for an army and an administration

questions.q:
Chitra's notes on a bazaar in a city of a vast territory read: 'A mint stamps one coin used in all the lands. Officers in the market collect tax. An army camp guards the border road. Traders from distant lands sell silk and spices.' She says: 'This proves the state is an empire and not just a kingdom.'
(a) Which feature of an empire does the mint show?
(b) Which features do the tax officers and the army camp show?
(c) Name one feature of the chapter's list that her notes do not mention.
(d) Does her evidence prove an empire? What further evidence would she need, and why?
questions.a: (a) Making laws and issuing currencies, weights and measures. (b) An administration (collecting taxes) and an army. (c) Any one of controlling resources, encouraging art and learning, communication networks, central authority over tributaries. (d) Not yet: a big kingdom may also have a mint and an army. She would need evidence that smaller territories keep their own rulers who pay tribute to the emperor in a capital.
s: Part (a): currency, weights and measures
Part (b): administration and army
Part (c): one unmentioned feature
Part (d): needs tributary rulers paying tribute as evidence

questions.q: 'An empire is held together by more than its army.' Justify the statement using the chapter.
questions.a: The army conquers tributaries and defends borders, but an administration with officials collects taxes and keeps order; laws, currencies and weights regulate trade; roads and river routes carry messages and goods; and encouragement of art, literature, religions and centres of learning is also a feature. The ruler also controls resources such as mines and forests.
s: Role of the army (control, expansion, defence)
Administration: officials, taxes, law and order
Laws, currency, weights and measures, regulating trade
Communication networks and infrastructure
Art, learning and resource control as further supports, with a conclusion

questions.q: Compare the position of an emperor and of a tributary ruler in an empire. Analyse what each gains from the arrangement.
questions.a: The emperor exerts central authority from a capital, receives tribute and loyalty and gains resources and power. The tributary king submits and accepts overlordship, pays tribute, but generally continues to govern his own area. Each gets something: the emperor wealth, power and control, the tributary a measure of self-rule.
s: Emperor: central authority, capital, overlord
Tributary: submits, pays tribute, accepts overlordship
Emperor's gains: tribute, resources, power
Tributary's gain: continues to govern own area
A clear comparison of the two positions

questions.q: (a) Name two things an emperor controls and regulates in economic life. (b) Why would a ruler want to control rivers and trade networks?
questions.a: (a) Any two of mines, forest produce, agricultural produce and manpower. (b) It gives control over precious resources and tax revenue from the trade.
s: Part (a): two resources or kinds of produce controlled
Part (b): control of resources and tax revenue from trade

questions.q: The word 'empire' comes from the Latin word imperium. What does imperium mean?
questions.a: Imperium means supreme power. 'Lord of all' is samraj, 'overlord' is adhiraja and 'king of kings' is rajadhiraja.
o: Supreme power
Lord of all
King of kings
Overlord

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a feature of an empire as described in the chapter?
questions.a: In return for tribute and loyalty, emperors generally allowed regional kings or chiefs to continue to govern their areas, so direct rule everywhere is not a listed feature.
o: Removes every tributary king and rules all regions directly
Makes laws and issues currencies, weights and measures
Maintains an army to keep tributary states under control
Designs an administration with officials to collect taxes and keep law and order

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tributary kings in an empire generally continued to govern their own areas.
Reason (R): The emperor ruled the whole territory from a capital, usually a major centre of economic and administrative power.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The capital fact is about where the emperor ruled from; it does not explain why tributary kings were allowed to keep governing.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by a tributary? (b) What did a tributary king receive in return for paying tribute and showing loyalty?
questions.a: (a) A ruler or state that has submitted to an emperor and pays tribute (money, grain, elephants and so on) as a sign of submission. (b) He was generally allowed to continue governing his own area.
s: Part (a): defines tributary as a submitted ruler who pays tribute
Part (b): continued to govern his own area

questions.q: Make up a short example of an empire of your own. Name an emperor, one tributary ruler with the tribute he sends, and the capital. Say which two features of an empire your example shows.
questions.a: Any consistent example, such as Emperor Mitra in capital Suvarnapur, with tributary king Arjun sending grain and elephants; shows tribute with own rulers, and a capital as centre, army or administration.
s: Names emperor, tributary and tribute plausibly
Names a capital as a centre of power
Names two features shown by the example

questions.q: A model of an ancient capital at a school fair shows a wide ditch around the walls, a bridge that can be pulled up, and a market selling silk, spices and gems from other regions. (a) What does the market show about the role of the capital? (b) What danger is the pull-up bridge meant for?
questions.a: (a) A capital is usually a major centre of economic power, drawing traders from distant lands. (b) A lifted bridge makes it harder to approach the fortifications when the city is in danger of attack.
s: Part (a): economic centre drawing traders
Part (b): defence against attack

questions.q: In the chapter, a tributary is best described as
questions.a: A tributary (vassal) pays tribute and accepts the emperor's overlordship. The governor is a satrap, the official is an emissary and the elected head belongs to a guild.
o: a ruler or state that has submitted to an emperor and pays tribute
a governor left behind by an overlord to manage far-off lands
an official sent abroad on a special mission of a diplomatic nature
the elected head of an association of traders and craftsmen

questions.q: Describe, with an example each, any three features of an empire.
questions.a: Any three: an army (to conquer and defend); an administration with officials (collect taxes, keep order); laws, currency, weights and measures; control of resources like mines and forests; encouragement of art and learning; communication networks like roads and river navigation.
s: Names an army function: conquer, defend, keep tributaries under control
Names an administration function: officials, taxes, law and order
Names a third feature (currency, resource control, communication or learning) with an example

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. Samraj  2. Adhiraja  3. Rajadhiraja  4. Imperium (Latin)
Column II: a. king of kings  b. supreme power  c. overlord  d. lord of all
questions.a: Samraj is lord of all, adhiraja is overlord, rajadhiraja is king of kings and imperium is supreme power.

questions.q:
Read the statements about empires.
Statement 1: Once a kingdom is part of an empire, its own ruler is always removed.
Statement 2: The emperor ruled the whole territory from a capital, usually a major centre of economic and administrative power.
Statement 3: Samraj means 'the lord of all' or 'supreme ruler'.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false: smaller territories still had their own rulers who paid tribute.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Differentiate between a kingdom and an empire in one line each.
questions.a: A kingdom is one territory under its own ruler. An empire is a collection of smaller kingdoms or territories under a powerful ruler to whom their own rulers pay tribute, ruled from a capital.
s: Describes a kingdom as a single territory with its ruler
Describes an empire as many territories under an emperor with tribute and a capital

questions.q: Give two purposes for which an empire maintained an army.
questions.a: To conquer neighbouring kingdoms and keep the tributary states under control; to defend the empire's borders from outside aggression.
s: First purpose: expand the empire or keep tributaries under control
Second purpose: protect against outside aggression

questions.q: A ruler orders one coin, one set of weights and measures and common trade rules in all the territories under him. Which feature of an empire is he showing?
questions.a: Issuing currency, fixing weights and measures and regulating trade are the 'makes laws' feature. The others are different features in the chapter's list.
o: Making laws and issuing currencies, weights and measures
Maintaining communication networks like roads and river navigation
Controlling access to mines, forests and manpower
Encouraging art, literature and centres of learning

questions.q:
Raja Suryadev of Suryapur is thinking of turning his kingdom into an empire. One minister says: 'Your name will be remembered for generations.' Another says: 'The hills around us hold mines and forests that can make us strong.' A third says: 'The neighbouring kingdoms' wealth will fill our treasury.' The treasurer warns that governing many distant territories needs a large army and many officials.
(a) Which word does the chapter use for 'the generations to come', and which minister's reason is closest to it?
(b) Which two things must an empire keep up, as the treasurer warns?
(c) Should Suryadev expand? Give one reason for and one cost against, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Posterity; the first minister. (b) An army and an administration (officials to manage territories, collect taxes, maintain law and order). (c) A reasoned decision citing one chapter motive (access to resources, wealth, ambition) and one cost (army, administration, hard to hold together).
s: Part (a): posterity and the first minister
Part (b): army and administration
Part (c): a decision citing one motive and one cost from the chapter

questions.q: Kabir says: 'In an empire the smaller kingdoms generally kept their own rulers, who paid tribute to the emperor.' Is Kabir right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the smaller territories still had their own rulers, who were tributaries to the emperor, and that in return for tribute and loyalty emperors generally allowed regional kings to govern their areas. The word 'generally' matters: the emperor still ruled the whole from a capital with an administration.
s: Verdict: agrees
Reason: tributaries kept their own rulers and paid tribute
Limit: the emperor ruled the whole from a capital with an administration

questions.q: King Veer of one kingdom defeats three neighbouring kingdoms. Their rulers keep governing their own lands but send grain and elephants to Veer's capital every year. What is Veer's position?
questions.a: Defeated rulers who keep their lands but pay tribute are tributaries, and the ruler they pay is an emperor.
o: An emperor who receives tribute from tributary rulers
The elected head of a guild that collects fees
A satrap who governs a province for an overlord
The ruler of a mahajanapada governed by assembly alone

questions.q: The chapter quotes an ancient text on who may lay down rules for their respective classes. Who are they?
questions.a: The text says cultivators, traders, herdsmen, moneylenders and artisans have authority to make rules for their classes, which is why the king was not to interfere.
o: The cultivators, traders and artisans themselves
The tributary kings governing each region of the empire
The satraps left behind by an overlord in far-off lands
The army chiefs who served the emperor in war

questions.q: (a) Besides guilds, which other institution does the chapter give as a sign of ancient India's self-organising ability? (b) What does it say happened to the spirit of the guilds after they ceased to exist formally?
questions.a: (a) The ancient village unit with its various committees and councils. (b) Their spirit continued to influence India's trade and business activities, sometimes even to this day.
s: Part (a): village committees and councils
Part (b): the spirit continued to influence trade and business

questions.q: A king plans a long campaign far from home. Soldiers must be fed, clothed, equipped and paid, and elephants and horses cared for, but his treasury is low. Which step does the chapter's reasoning support for raising money in the long run?
questions.a: The chapter says production and trade bring more income for producers and increased tax for the ruler, and that guilds helped trade flourish. Raising tribute is a different, short-term method, and the chapter does not present it as the way to pay for armies.
o: Encourage production and trade so that more tax comes in
Close the trade routes so that all goods stay inside his kingdom
Abolish guilds so that merchants compete against each other
Raise the tribute demanded from the conquered kings

questions.q:
A king plans a 90-day campaign. His clerk's bill lists: food, cloth and pay for 5,000 soldiers at 3 coins a day each, and fodder for 200 elephants at 20 coins a day each. Caravan tax on the trade routes brings in about 8,000 coins a day.
(a) Which army costs named in the chapter are missing from the clerk's bill?
(b) What is the total bill for 90 days, and how much of it does the caravan tax cover?
(c) The minister suggests postponing the campaign to improve trade, or asking tributaries for more tribute. Which would you advise, and why?
questions.a: (a) Weapons and equipment, care of horses, and building roads or ships. (b) Soldiers 5000 x 3 x 90 = 13,50,000; elephants 200 x 20 x 90 = 3,60,000; total 17,10,000 coins; tax 8000 x 90 = 7,20,000, leaving 9,90,000 uncovered. (c) Either, with reasons: postponing lets production and trade grow, which raises income and tax; more tribute is quicker but can burden local rulers and breed resentment.
s: Part (a): equipment, horses or roads and ships missing from the bill
Part (b): 17,10,000 total and 7,20,000 covered
Part (c): a justified decision using trade income or tribute resentment

questions.q: Why was the king not supposed to interfere in the internal rules of a guild?
questions.a: The guilds had autonomy to create their own rules, an ancient text gave classes the authority to lay down rules, and an enlightened ruler lets people organise themselves when local institutions work well and trade flourishes.
s: Guilds had autonomy to make rules
Reason: trade flourished so interference was unneeded

questions.q: Write a short notice that a guild in a trading town might put up, showing how it was organised. Mention who leads it, who helps him and one rule the guild makes for itself.
questions.a: A notice such as: 'The guild of Kaveri port is led by its elected head Kumaran with two executive officers; no member may sell below the agreed price of pepper.' It shows an elected head, executive officers and a self-made rule.
s: Names an elected head
Names executive officers
Gives an internal rule the guild itself makes

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: 'Guilds helped both the traders and the king.' Give two points for each.
questions.a: Traders: they collaborated rather than competed, shared information, and made their own rules with an elected head. The king: flourishing trade brought more tax, and he did not have to interfere, which an enlightened ruler would avoid when institutions work. Guilds endured for centuries, so both gained.
s: Trader point 1: collaboration and sharing information
Trader point 2: autonomy and elected head
King point 1: more trade means more tax
King point 2: no need to interfere in working institutions
Judgement that both gained, with evidence of long life

questions.q: 'Production and trade are as important as the army for running an empire.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: An army is costly: soldiers must be fed, clothed, equipped and paid, elephants and horses cared for, roads or ships built. This needs economic power. Controlling trade routes increases the goods traded, income of producers and the ruler's tax. Goods like textiles, spices and gems moved by land and sea, and guilds organised the traders, so a flourishing economy paid for the army.
s: Army is costly: names expenses
Economic power is needed to meet them
Trade routes and goods raise income and taxes
Guilds organised traders and helped trade flourish
Concludes that the army depends on the economy

questions.q: In the chapter, the word for a guild of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders or agriculturists is
questions.a: Guilds are shrenis. Saptanga is Kautilya's seven parts of a kingdom, satraps are provincial governors and sutras are concise phrases of knowledge.
o: shrenis
saptanga
satraps
sutras

questions.q: Why is maintaining an army a costly affair? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Soldiers need to be fed, clothed, equipped with weapons and paid; elephants and horses must be cared for; roads or ships have to be built.
s: Names a cost of the soldiers: feeding, clothing, equipping or paying them
Names a second cost: caring for elephants and horses, or building roads and ships

questions.q: A weaver, a spice seller and a moneylender in Kaushambi form a body. They vote for a head, appoint two officers and make their own rules for trade, while the king does not interfere. What would the chapter call this body?
questions.a: A voluntary association of traders and craftsmen with an elected head and its own rules is a guild (shreni).
o: A guild, a self-ruling body of traders
A village council, a committee that ran one village
A saptanga, the seven parts that make a kingdom
A tributary state, a kingdom that pays tribute

questions.q: According to the chapter, why is trade so important to a ruler who wants to run an empire?
questions.a: The chapter says more trade means more income for producers and increased tax collection for the ruler. It does not say trade replaces the army or tribute, and it calls production and trade 'one of the keys', not the only one.
o: It raises producers' income and the ruler's tax
Trade lets the ruler stop keeping an army altogether
Trade makes tribute from other kings unnecessary
Trade is the only activity that can sustain an empire

questions.q: (a) Name the two trade routes the chapter's map asks you to notice. (b) Goods travelled by land and by sea; why would a ruler want to control the routes on which they moved?
questions.a: (a) The Uttarapatha and the Dakshinapatha. (b) More goods traded means more income for producers and increased tax collections for the ruler.
s: Part (a): Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha
Part (b): control of routes raises income and tax

questions.q:
Read the statements about guilds.
Statement 1: Guilds brought together people who ended up as collaborators rather than competitors.
Statement 2: The king drew up the rules of every guild and appointed its head.
Statement 3: Guilds spread over large parts of India and endured for centuries.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: a guild's head was usually elected and the guilds had the autonomy to make their own rules.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Which of these was NOT a group that formed guilds, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Guilds were associations of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders or agriculturists. Soldiers are not listed.
o: Soldiers of the empire's army
Craftsmen working in the towns
Moneylenders who lent to traders
Agriculturists who tilled the land

questions.q: (a) Name any three goods traded in ancient India. (b) Explain why a wider variety and quantity of goods improved the ruler's income.
questions.a: (a) Any three of textiles, spices, agricultural produce, gems, handicrafts, animals. (b) More trade means more income for producers and more tax collected by the ruler.
s: Part (a): three correct trade goods
Part (b): more trade gives more tax collections

questions.q: Explain how trade benefits (i) producers, (ii) the ruler and (iii) the people of an empire, as the chapter describes.
questions.a: (i) More trade means more income for producers. (ii) It brings increased tax collection for the ruler. (iii) Economic activity ensures people's welfare and quality of life, which a good ruler should be concerned with.
s: Benefit to producers
Benefit to the ruler
Benefit to the people's welfare

questions.q: Anita says: 'Guilds made traders who might have been competitors into collaborators, and that is why guilds lasted for centuries.' Is she completely right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly. The chapter says guilds brought together people who ended up as collaborators rather than competitors, and that they spread widely and endured for centuries. But it names a second remarkable feature, autonomy to make their own rules, and does not say that collaboration alone was the reason for their long life.
s: Verdict: right about collaboration, not completely right
Supports: collaborators rather than competitors; guilds endured for centuries
Limit: autonomy is the second feature, and the chapter does not give one reason for their long life

questions.q:
Two towns on the Ganga each had 60 cloth makers. In Town A they sold separately and kept their prices and wages secret; the price of a bolt of cloth fell from 40 to 28 coins in a season. In Town B the cloth makers and local moneylenders chose a head, and met to share what they knew about markets, supply and demand and workers; their price fell from 40 only to 36 coins.
(a) What does the chapter call the body formed in Town B, and how was its head usually chosen?
(b) What did sharing information turn the members from, and into?
(c) By what percentage did the price fall in Town A and in Town B, and which chapter idea explains the difference?
(d) A royal officer wants to fix cloth prices in both towns. Advise the king, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A guild (shreni); its head was usually elected. (b) From competitors into collaborators. (c) Town A: 12 on 40 = 30%; Town B: 4 on 40 = 10%; collaboration in sharing information. (d) Either, with the chapter's reasons: guilds had autonomy and the king was not to interfere when trade flourishes; or Town A's fall shows producers can suffer, but the better answer is to encourage the guild model in Town A rather than fix prices.
s: Part (a): guild and elected head
Part (b): competitors into collaborators
Part (c): 30% and 10% with collaboration as the idea
Part (d): a decision citing autonomy and non-interference or the benefit of cooperation

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Traders joined together in guilds instead of working only as isolated individuals.
Reason (R): Sharing resources and information on markets, supply and demand and workforce was to everyone's benefit.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the benefits of sharing information and resources are why traders joined forces.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
In a village of 50 families in Magadha, each family harvested 40 sacks of grain a year and needed 38 for itself. After 20 families took up iron-tipped ploughs, those 20 families harvested 55 sacks each, while the other 30 families still harvested 40. Assume the local chief collects the extra grain produced by the new ploughs.
(a) What does the chapter say iron ploughs did for agriculture?
(b) Find the village's total surplus before and after the 20 families changed their ploughs.
(c) What does the chapter say a food surplus allows people to do?
(d) The chief can use the extra grain either to support more soldiers with iron weapons or about 7 craftsman families (taking 38 sacks to feed a family). Which would you recommend, and why?
questions.a: (a) They increased agricultural produce. (b) Before: 50 x 2 = 100 sacks. After: 20 x 17 + 30 x 2 = 340 + 60 = 400 sacks. (c) More people can focus on arts and crafts, which are in demand inside and outside the empire. (d) 300 sacks feed 7 whole families at 38 sacks each. Either, with reasons: craftsmen produce goods for trade and raise income, which the chapter links to Magadha's rise; soldiers with iron weapons strengthen the army.
s: Part (a): iron ploughs raised produce
Part (b): 100 sacks before and 400 after
Part (c): surplus lets people focus on arts and crafts
Part (d): a justified choice using the chapter

questions.q:
Read the statements about Magadha and the Nandas.
Statement 1: Ajatashatru helped make Magadha a dominant centre of power, and the Buddha and Mahavira lived in his time.
Statement 2: Mahapadma Nanda united many smaller kingdoms and extended his empire across parts of eastern and northern India.
Statement 3: Mahapadma Nanda founded the Nanda dynasty around the 4th century BCE.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: The first two statements are correct. The third is false: the chapter places Mahapadma Nanda around the 5th century BCE.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Who was Panini? Name his work and say how many sutras it has.
questions.a: Panini was a famed Sanskrit grammarian of about the 5th century BCE, in the time of the Nandas. His work is the Ashtadhyayi, which lists the rules of Sanskrit grammar in 3,996 short sutras.
s: Identifies Panini as a Sanskrit grammarian and his work
Gives 3,996 sutras

questions.q: (a) Name two natural resources that helped Magadha rise. (b) Explain how iron ore changed farming and the army of Magadha.
questions.a: (a) Any two of fertile land, forests (timber), elephants, iron ore and minerals from hills. (b) Iron ploughs increased agricultural produce, and lighter, sharper iron weapons strengthened the army.
s: Part (a): two resources of Magadha
Part (b): iron ploughs for farming and iron weapons for the army

questions.q: Who founded the Nanda dynasty in Magadha around the 5th century BCE?
questions.a: Mahapadma Nanda founded the dynasty. Dhana Nanda was its last emperor, Ajatashatru was an earlier Magadhan king and Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas.
o: Mahapadma Nanda
Ajatashatru
Dhana Nanda
Chandragupta Maurya

questions.q: Describe a short imagined scene from a Magadhan village that shows how iron ploughs could end up raising the king's income. Show at least three links in the chain.
questions.a: A scene such as: an iron plough digs deeper, harvest rises, extra grain lets a family's son become a potter, pots are carried down the Son river and sold, and the king collects more income. It shows ploughs, surplus, crafts and trade as links.
s: Iron plough raises produce
Surplus lets people work in crafts
Trade by river raises income

questions.q: Rahul says: 'The Nanda empire fell because it was poor and had no army.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Dhana Nanda was very rich, and Greek accounts say the Nandas kept a large army. The chapter says he became highly unpopular because he oppressed and exploited his people, which paved the way for the Mauryas to conquer and absorb the empire.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Evidence: the last ruler was rich and the Nandas had a large army
Cause given by the chapter: unpopularity from oppression and exploitation

questions.q: A king of Magadha wants lighter, sharper weapons for his soldiers and elephants for his army. Which two features of his kingdom supply these, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Iron ore and minerals from nearby hills gave weapons, and forests supplied elephants. Rivers and surplus grain help trade and food, not weapons and elephants directly.
o: Iron ore from nearby hills and elephants from the forests
The Ganga and Son rivers and the surplus of food grains
Punch-marked silver coins and Panini's rules of grammar
Fertile plains and the Great Stupa at Sanchi

questions.q: What do (i) his coins, (ii) the Greek accounts of his army and (iii) the extent of his empire tell us about Mahapadma Nanda?
questions.a: (i) He issued coins, showing economic power in a thriving economy. (ii) Greek accounts say the Nandas kept a large army. (iii) He unified many smaller kingdoms and extended his empire across parts of eastern and northern India.
s: Coins show economic power
Large army from Greek accounts
Unified kingdoms across eastern and northern India

questions.q: In a Magadhan village, a family changes from a simple plough to one with an iron tip. Its harvest grows and some villagers now make pots and cloth instead of farming. Which chain does the chapter support?
questions.a: The chapter says iron ploughs raised produce, and surplus food grains allowed more people to focus on arts and crafts that were in demand inside and outside the empire.
o: Higher yield gave a surplus, so more people could take up crafts
Higher yield made craftsmen return to farming to meet tribute
A surplus of grain removed the need for trade with other lands
Iron tools improved yields but did nothing for arts and crafts

questions.q: (a) What did Ajatashatru do for Magadha? (b) Which two famous religious figures lived in his time, and in which Grade 6 chapter does the book tell you to revisit their teachings?
questions.a: (a) He played a crucial role in establishing Magadha as a dominant centre of power. (b) The Buddha and Mahavira; 'India's Cultural Roots'.
s: Part (a): made Magadha a dominant centre of power
Part (b): Buddha and Mahavira, India's Cultural Roots

questions.q: Explain why Magadha, between the 6th and the 4th century BCE, rose in importance and set the stage for India's first empire. Give at least four factors.
questions.a: Magadha lay in the resource-rich Ganga plains with fertile land, forests for timber and elephants. Iron ore from nearby hills gave iron ploughs and weapons. Surplus grain supported arts and crafts. The Ganga and Son rivers carried trade, boosting its income. Strong early kings like Ajatashatru made it a centre of power.
s: Fertile land, forests and elephants
Iron ore leading to iron ploughs and weapons
Surplus food supporting arts and crafts
Rivers used for transport and trade income
Role of early kings like Ajatashatru

questions.q: State two things that show the strength of Mahapadma Nanda's rule.
questions.a: He united many smaller kingdoms and extended his empire across parts of eastern and northern India; he issued coins, showing economic power; Greek accounts say the Nandas kept a large army.
s: First sign of strength
Second sign of strength

questions.q:
Match the person in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Ajatashatru  2. Mahapadma Nanda  3. Dhana Nanda  4. Panini
Column II: a. Composed the Ashtadhyayi  b. Founded the Nanda dynasty and issued coins  c. Last Nanda emperor, very rich but unpopular  d. Early Magadhan king in whose time the Buddha and Mahavira lived
questions.a: Ajatashatru-early king; Mahapadma Nanda-founder and coins; Dhana Nanda-last emperor; Panini-Ashtadhyayi.

questions.q: Why were the Ganga and Son rivers an advantage for Magadha?
questions.a: The chapter says the rivers gave a geographical advantage for trade as they could be used for transport. Iron ore came from nearby hills and elephants and timber from the forests.
o: They could carry goods, boosting trade and income

Favours for those who benefit the people in villages
The people's interest comes first

questions.q: The word 'Arthashastra' literally means

the art of war and diplomacy among kings

questions.q: A kingdom has a wise king, loyal ministers, strong forts and fertile villages. But its treasury has run dry and its neighbours have all turned away from it. Which two parts of the saptanga are in trouble?

Durga and danda

questions.q: Differentiate between a language and a script using Ashoka's edicts as the example.

questions.q: Ashoka is called a 'great communicator' who cared for his subjects. Justify this statement using the chapter.
